div.head: SUBSECT. 5.
Old age a cause.
div.p:
Secondary peculiar causes, efficient, so called in respect of the other precedent, are either congenitae, internae, innatae as they term them, inward, innate, and inbred; or else outward and adventitious, which happen to us, after we are born: congenite or born with us, are either natural, as old age, or praeter naturam [against nature] (as Lib. 1 Path. cap. 11.Fernelius calls it), that distemperature, which we have from our Parents’ seed, it being an hereditary disease. The first of these, which is natural to all, and which no man living can avoid, is Venit enim properata malis inopina senectus & dolor aetatem jussit inesse meam [For old age came unexpectedly, hastened by misfortunes, and grief has decreed that its lifetime would be attached to mine]. Boethius met. 1 de consol. Philos.old age, which being cold and dry, and of the same quality as Melancholy is, must needs cause it, by diminution of spirits and substance, and increasing of adust humours; therefore Cap. de humoribus, lib. de Anima.Melanchthon avers out of Aristotle, as an undoubted truth, Senes plerunque delirasse in senecta, that old men familiarly dote, ob atram bilem, for black choler, which is then superabundant in them: and Rhasis that Arabian Physician in his Cont. lib. 1 cap. 9, calls it a necessary and inseparable accident, to all old and decrepit persons. After Psal. 90. 10.70 years (as the Psalmist saith) all is trouble and sorrow; and common experience confirms the truth of it in weak old persons, especially in such as have lived in action all their lives, had great employment, much business, much command, and many servants to oversee, and leave off ex abrupto [without warning]; as Meteran Belg. hist. lib. 1.Charles the fifth did to King Philip, resign up all on a sudden; they are overcome with melancholy in an instant: or if they do continue in such courses, they dote at last (senex bis puer [the old man’s twice a boy]), and are not able to manage their estates through common infirmities incident to their age; full of ache, sorrow and grief, Children again, dizzards, they Carl many times as they sit, and talk to themselves, they are angry, waspish, displeased with everything, suspicious of all, wayward, covetous, hard (saith Tull. de senectute.Tully), self-willed, superstitious, self-conceited, braggers and admirers of themselves, as Lib. 2 de Aulico. Senes avari, morosi, jactabundi, philauti, deliri, superstitiosi, suspitiosi, &c. [Old men {are} greedy, peevish, boastful, selfish, doting, superstitious, suspicious, etc.]Balthasar Castilio hath truly noted of them. This natural infirmity is most eminent in old women, and such as are poor, solitary, live in most base esteem and beggary, or such as are Witches; insomuch that Lib. 3 de Lamiis, cap. 17 et 18.Wierus, Baptista Porta, Ulricus Molitor, Ewichius, do refer all that witches are said to do, to
Imagination alone, and this humour of melancholy. And whereas it is controverted, whether they can bewitch cattle to death, ride in the air upon a Coul-staff out of a Chimney-top, transform themselves into Cats, Dogs, &c., translate bodies from place to place, meet in companies, and dance, as they do, or have carnal copulation with the Devil, they ascribe all to this redundant melancholy, which domineers in them, to Solanum, opium, lupi adeps, lac asini, &c., sanguis infantum, &c. [Nightshade, opium, wolf-fat, asses’ milk, etc., the blood of infants, etc.]somniferous potions, and natural causes, the Devil’s policy. Non laedunt omnino (saith Wierus) aut quid mirum faciunt (de Lamiis lib. 3 cap. 36) ut putatur, solam vitiatam habent phantasiam [They do no harm at all … or anything extraordinary … as is believed; they just have a faulty fantasy]; they do no such wonders at all, only their Corrupta est iis ab humore Melancholico phantasia [The fantasy is corrupted in them by the melancholic humour], Nymannus.Brains are crazed. They think they are Witches, and can do hurt, but do not. But this opinion Bodin, Erastus, Danaeus, Scribanius, Sebastian Michaelis, Campanella de Sensu rerum lib. 4 cap. 9, Qui haec in Imaginationis vim referre conati sunt, aut atrae bilis, inanem prorsus laborem susceperunt [Those who have attempted to ascribe these things to the force of the imagination, or of black bile, have undertaken an utterly worthless task].Dandinus the Jesuit, lib. 2 de Anima, explode; Lib. 4 cap. 4 omnif. mag.Cicogna confutes at large. That Witches are melancholy, they deny not, but not out of corrupt fantasy alone, so to delude themselves and others, or to produce such effects.
